topic.title: Why 'The Simpsons predicted it' spreads
topic.claim: We share 'The Simpsons predicted it' because a coincidence with a script feels safer than a world where things just happen.
topic.behaviour: A cartoon clip resurfaces on the same day as a real outage. People send it around as proof that someone knew in advance.
topic.mechanism: A pattern is easier to bear than chaos, and a prediction clip is easy to post. The people who post it get reach without having to check anything.
topic.group: Heavy Instagram and X users who forward clips to friends
topic.moment: A friend sends you a clip with 'bro, look at the date' and nothing else.

turn.believed: The clip is spooky because it matches the news.
turn.actually: It matches because we went looking for the match. The details that don't fit never get posted.

topic.feeling: a bit foolish for almost believing it
topic.villain: a feed that rewards the spookiest version of a coincidence
topic.because: A spooky post earns shares, and shares are the point. Checking would kill the post.

proof.fact: A clip from the 2023 Simpsons episode 'It's A Blunderful Life' shows an older Lisa writing about a blackout in her diary, dated November 17. Skeptics noted that Lisa's diary never mentions 2026.

topic.payoff: A prediction that needs three real events and one missing year to work is not a prediction.
topic.send_to: The friend who forwards every 'they knew' clip
real_details: It resurfaced alongside a Microsoft outage and a scheduled US emergency alert test on the same date
topic.news_peg: The Simpsons blackout clip resurfaced on 17 November 2026
topic.why_now: The clip went viral on 17 November and the pattern repeats with every big news day.

reader.point: People believe 'The Simpsons predicted it' because the clips are vague, lack a year, and get shared without checking, so it's not real prediction but our brains and group chats filling in the gaps.
reader.reason: A scary-news environment makes people crave the relief of 'someone knew', and spooky clips get shared more than they get checked.

sources.fact: The Simpsons episode behind the November 2026 blackout clip has no documented reference to November 2026. The real 17 November event was a scheduled FEMA/FCC Emergency Alert System test, not a power outage.
sources.stance: supports: the page checks the clip and finds the 'prediction' unverified, so a post that shares it without checking would be passing on something that doesn't hold up. It says nothing about why people share it.
sources.excerpt: The clip comes from "It's a Blunderful Life," which first aired on November 19, 2023. The claim about the episode's final 15 seconds "has not been independently verified." The episode "contains no documented reference to November 2026". FEMA and the FCC scheduled a nationwide Emergency Alert System test for about 2:20 p.m. Eastern on November 17, 2026. The test message "state[s] that no public action is required." Neither the FCC nor FEMA documentation describes a planned power outage.

sources.fact: An Indian outlet found that a viral 'Simpsons predicted an internet blackout' clip was AI-generated and not from the show. The date it named also didn't match the event it was supposedly predicting.
sources.stance: supports: it shows these viral 'prediction' clips can be fabricated and are easily debunked, so checking would undermine the post. It is a January 2025 case, not the November 2026 clip, and it doesn't address why people share them.
sources.excerpt: "the visuals aren't derived from the episodes of the American show 'The Simpsons' but are, instead, an AI-generated one." It "does not accurately represent any episode of the original show". It "is learned to be purely produced using artificial intelligence". The article also says the Trump inauguration clip didn't match the actual date, January 20 rather than the 16th.

cover.headline: [Simpsons predictions] are matches we make ourselves, then forward
cover.sub: The cartoon gave a date. We supplied the rest.

paragraphs: "The Simpsons predicted it" clips aren't predictions. We make the match ourselves, then forward it.
slides.why_swipe: How do we make the match?

paragraphs: A friend sends you a clip. The only text: "bro, look at the date."
It's from a 2023 Simpsons episode, where a grown-up Lisa writes in her diary about a blackout dated November 17.
slides.why_swipe: So what's wrong with the date?

paragraphs: Look at what the diary leaves out. It says November 17. It never says 2026.
The year in your head came from you, not the show.
slides.why_swipe: And did a blackout even happen?

paragraphs: On 17 November 2026, the US didn't have a blackout. It had a scheduled emergency alert test.
Its message said no public action is required.
slides.why_swipe: Then why did everyone forward it?

paragraphs: Because the spooky version is the one that gets replies. You feel a small chill, and the clip is gone in four seconds.
You've typed "bhai WHAT" back before checking a single thing.
A two-minute check would turn it into nothing. And nothing gets no replies.
A diary date, an alert test, and a year nobody wrote. That's not a prediction.
It's the group chat doing the cartoon's homework.

draft.alt_text: A text-only Instagram carousel of eight slides arguing that 'The Simpsons predicted it' clips aren't predictions: we make the match ourselves, then forward it. It uses the November 2026 clip from a 2023 Simpsons episode where a grown-up Lisa writes about a blackout in her diary dated November 17. The diary never says 2026, and on 17 November 2026 the US had a scheduled emergency alert test, not a blackout, whose message said no public action is required. It says people forward the clip because the spooky version gets replies, and we type 'bhai WHAT' before checking anything, while a check would turn it into nothing. It ends by listing a diary date, an alert test and a year nobody wrote, and calling it the group chat doing the cartoon's homework.

claims.text: The clip comes from a 2023 Simpsons episode and shows an older Lisa writing about a blackout in her diary, dated November 17.
The real US event on 17 November 2026 was a scheduled emergency alert test, not a blackout.
The emergency alert test message said no public action is required.
